title: Show HN: CheckOwners to find your repo's hidden single points of failure
author: smusali
body:
Hey HN Community!I created checkOwners to solve a problem by many engineering teams: who knows your codebase, and what will happen when they go away?This is an open-source, local-first tool which performs analysis based on Git history in order to find hidden knowledge risk in repositories.It is able to recognize true experts, recognize out-of-date ownership definitions, find knowledge bottlenecks, propose review candidates, and model what would happen when contributors go away.All the magic happens on your own local system without uploading source code or an LLM. It also works within GitHub Actions.Try it:
```
pip install checkowners
checkowners audit
checkowners risk
```Would appreciate any feedback from maintainers and platform engineers regarding the accuracy of Git history reflection of expertise and findings of risk analysis.

comments.author: the_shivers
comments.text: Hey everyone. My previous daily game, enclose.horse, was a surprising success, so I figured I'd take a stab at making another.Tower of Questions is a high-stakes daily trivia game. Seven multiple-choice questions, each harder than the last, and if you get one wrong, you die!While there are other daily trivia games out there, I felt they were lacking in excitement; if I got a question wrong, my reaction was "so what?" I wanted to see if I could make a trivia game where a wrong answer was actually terrifying. The obvious way to do this is by making a wrong answer an instant loss. Of course, that’s a bit harsh: you might be great at trivia, but one question in your weakest category can end your run. My solution was to give players lifelin—I mean “relics.” Long story short, I ended up remaking Who Wants to Be A Millionaire from first principles. Although I think "daily Who Wants to Be A Millionaire" is actually a pretty compelling pitch!I'm also rebelling against the daily game trend of "minimalist everything, rounded rectangles everywhere." Every game seems to want to be a Wordle clone, so I went in the complete opposite direction. I spent about 6 weeks making all the pixel art for this. While I have some regrets about it, I think the result looks pretty cool.Anyway, give it a play and let me know what you think! I would love any feedback, whether it be about performance, question difficulty, or anything else you might notice.

## README

# ⚡ AirFlick Drop

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

> **The zero-friction, cross-platform AirDrop alternative for Windows, Android, and iOS.** 
> Flick photos, 4K videos, and files up to **15 GB** from any phone to your computer with zero-RAM chunked streaming, 3D physics gestures, smart Bump-to-Top placement, and **zero app installs on mobile**.

 
 
 🌐 Open Live Web App (Permanent Domain) 
 
 

---

## 🌟 The Cross-Ecosystem Breakdown

Apple AirDrop is brilliant inside the Apple walled garden, but completely breaks down across platforms:
- ❌ **iPhone ➔ Windows**: AirDrop does not exist on Windows. Users resort to slow cables, WhatsApp compression, or emailing files to themselves.
- ❌ **Android ➔ Mac**: Quick Share doesn't work on macOS.
- ❌ **Snapdrop / WebRTC Clones**: Disconnect constantly when networks switch, freeze on files over 500 MB, and require both devices on the exact same router.

**AirFlick Drop fixes all of them permanently:**
- 📱 **Send from ANY Phone**: iPhone (Safari), iPad, Android (Chrome, Samsung Internet) — **Zero apps to install**!
- 💻 **Receive on Windows**: Desktop companion with silent Windows startup, auto-detecting Wi-Fi/Hotspot transitions, and Desktop Bump-to-Top sorting.
- 🌐 **Works Anywhere**: Seamlessly switches between **100% Offline Local Wi-Fi** (0 MB internet) and **Worldwide 5G/Mobile Data** (via secure Cloudflare Tunnel).

---

## 📊 Feature Comparison: Why AirFlick Drop?

| Feature | AirFlick Drop ⚡ | Apple AirDrop 🍎 | Samsung / Google Quick Share 📱 | Snapdrop / ShareDrop 🌐 |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Windows 10/11 Support** | ✅ **Native Companion** | ❌ No | ⚠️ Windows App Only | ⚠️ Browser Only |
| **iPhone ➔ Windows** | ✅ **Native Zero-Lag** | ❌ Impossible | ❌ Impossible | ⚠️ Drops connections |
| **Android ➔ Windows** | ✅ **Instant** | ❌ Impossible | ⚠️ Same account needed | ⚠️ WebRTC freezes |
| **Mobile App Install** | ❌ **Zero (PWA Web)** | ⚠️ Built-in iOS only | ⚠️ Android only | ❌ Zero |
| **Max File Size** | 🚀 **Up to 15 GB** | ⚠️ ~4 GB practical | ⚠️ 3 GB limit | ❌ Crashes >500 MB |
| **Different Networks (5G)**| ✅ **Full 5G Support** | ❌ Same Wi-Fi only | ❌ Same Wi-Fi only | ❌ Same Wi-Fi only |
| **100% Offline (No Internet)**| ✅ **Local Wi-Fi / Hotspot** | ✅ Ad-hoc Wi-Fi | ⚠️ Needs Bluetooth handshake | ❌ Needs signaling server |
| **Desktop Auto-Sort** | ✅ **Smart Bump-to-Top** | ❌ Dumps into Downloads | ❌ Dumps into Downloads | ❌ Dumps into Downloads |
| **Device Pairing & Privacy** | 🛡️ **Cryptographic Token** | ⚠️ Broadcasts to contacts | ⚠️ Account required | ❌ Public / Unsecured |

---

## 🚀 Key Features

* **📱 Flick-to-Screen Gestures**: Drag the file card and flick upward toward your computer screen with real-time 3D tilt perspective, Web Audio synthesized whoosh effects, and physical haptic feedback.
* **⚡ 15 GB Large File Streaming**: Uses 4MB chunked streaming over local HTTP. Files stream directly to disk without bloating mobile or laptop RAM.
* **⏸ Pause, Resume & Cancel**: Real-time Transfer HUD with live MB/s speed, progress bar, `⏸ Pause` / `▶ Resume`, and `✕ Cancel` (with automatic partial file cleanup).
* **🚀 Smart Bump-to-Top on Desktop**: When a file lands on Desktop, AirFlick silently refreshes its timestamp to the current second so it immediately appears at the top of your Desktop grid.
* **🛡️ Zero Data Breach Security**: Server only accepts uploads; it contains **zero file-browsing or download endpoints**. Unpaired strangers are rejected with `401 Unauthorized`.
* **🔄 Dual-Engine Connectivity**:
 * **Online Mode (Anywhere)**: Connects across 5G/Mobile Data and home Wi-Fi via secure Cloudflare Tunnel.
 * **Offline Mode (100% Offline)**: Connects over local Wi-Fi router or laptop Hotspot with zero internet required.
* **🔌 Silent Windows Autostart**: Launches silently in the Windows system tray on boot — zero black terminal windows or annoying popups.

---

## 🛠️ Architecture

```
airflick-drop/
├── main_window.py      # PyQt6 desktop GUI (QR code, network change listener, tray)
├── server.py           # Flask HTTP chunked streaming server (CORS + Token auth)
├── tunnel.py           # Cloudflare Tunnel manager with auto-sync to cloud Gist
├── autostart.py        # Windows Startup registration (StartAirFlick.vbs)
├── web/                # Mobile client PWA web app (served via GitHub Pages)
│   ├── index.html      # Mobile UI with 3D flick physics & full-fit preview
│   ├── manifest.json   # PWA manifest with native AirFlick icon
│   ├── sw.js           # Offline service worker cache
│   └── icon.png        # 512x512 app icon
├── tests/              # Automated unit test suite (pytest)
│   ├── test_server.py  # Server endpoint tests
│   └── test_tunnel.py  # Tunnel binary and health tests
├── docs/               # System documentation
│   ├── ARCHITECTURE.md # Network topology & data flow
│   └── TROUBLESHOOTING.md # Comprehensive troubleshooting guide
└── scripts/
    └── doctor.py       # Automated diagnostic health-check CLI tool
```

---

## 🚀 Quickstart

### 1. Prerequisites
* Python 3.10+
* Windows 10/11, macOS, or Linux
* Any modern mobile browser (iOS Safari, Android Chrome, Samsung Internet)

### 2. Installation
```bash
git clone https://github.com/k39139215-gif/airflick-drop.git
cd airflick-drop
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### 3. Run AirFlick
**On Windows:**
```bash
python main_window.py
```
*(AirFlick will also automatically install a silent Windows startup launcher so it runs in the background on every reboot).*

### 4. Connect Phone
1. Scan the QR code displayed on the companion window with your phone's camera.
2. Pick any photo, document, or huge 4K video.
3. **Flick it up toward your screen** — it lands on your computer's Desktop instantly!

---

## ❓ Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

### Can I transfer files from iPhone to Windows without iTunes or cables?
Yes! AirFlick Drop works directly in iOS Safari with zero app installs. Simply open the QR code or link, pick your photos/videos from the native iOS picker, and flick them to your Windows PC.

### Does AirFlick Drop compress my 4K videos or photos?
No. Unlike WhatsApp or Telegram which compress your photos, AirFlick Drop transfers the exact raw byte stream untouched with 100% original quality.

### Does it work when my internet is offline?
Yes! Connect both devices to the same Wi-Fi router (even with no internet connection) or turn on your laptop's Mobile Hotspot. AirFlick will transfer directly over local Wi-Fi waves at up to 80 MB/s.

### Is my data safe from strangers?
Yes. AirFlick server has zero file-browsing or download endpoints — your computer files can never be viewed from the outside. In addition, every desktop generates a cryptographic pairing token so only your paired phone can flick files.

## README

# Nouli

**Every decision has a history.**

Keep the facts behind a decision, add what changes, and ask the next question without losing the earlier answer. Nouli is a terminal app, CLI, and Rust library for connected decision histories: a ledger-backed decision network. Use a compatible decision service, or follow a task-specific model’s local recipe. Use the CLI to run individual model requests with a recorded decision history.

CI Release Total downloads across all release assets License: MIT Rust 1.99.1+

Website · Models · Quickstart · Examples · User guide

## See Nouli in action

Nouli TUI replay: saved decisions, branches, and blends.

*Current terminal app, replaying saved workshop answers at 3× speed. Watch the video or inspect the recording.*

## Quickstart

Install the CLI on Apple silicon macOS:

```sh
brew install nouli-ai/tap/nouli
```

On GNU/Linux, or Apple silicon macOS without Homebrew:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://nouli.ai/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

Then choose a starting path:

- **Run a Nouli model locally:** choose a task-specific model and follow its model card to set up the environment, load weights, start the local service, and run the supplied CLI workflow.
- **Ask broader decision questions:** connect an appropriate general-purpose decision service, choose a model, then open the terminal app:

```sh
nouli connect
nouli
```

In the app, add facts in **Context** and write a plain question in **Question**. **Enter** adds a nonempty context row; Enter on a blank row moves to the next section. **Shift-Tab** changes the answer type and **Tab** moves between sections. Send with **Enter** on a nonempty Question or **Ctrl-S** from any section. Options/Levels use one item per row; blank Enter finishes the list without sending. Use `/exit` to return to your shell. Terminal guide.

A service must support System One or OpenAI Decisions. Provider fees may apply to remote inference. Connection setup.

Prebuilt CLI binaries support Apple silicon macOS and ARM64/x86_64 GNU/Linux with glibc 2.38+. The download installer checks its checksum and installs into `~/.local/bin` by default. Each local model has its own runtime requirements. Installation and upgrades.

## Work in the terminal

- **Choose a model without losing your draft.** Open `/model` or press **Ctrl-L** to search your connections, add one, or enter a missing API key. The selected model stays available in later views.
- **Reuse saved answers and files.** Type `@` to search local history or attach a file. Review its snapshot before sending; references connect the saved source to the new decision.
- **Copy and resize.** Drag normally to select text and use terminal Copy. **Ctrl-P** holds the view while a request continues; Esc resumes. For panel resizing, press **Ctrl-G**, drag the divider, then press **Esc** to return to the form and native selection.
- **Choose what the status line shows.** Use `/statusline` for the Minimal, Session, Request, or Hidden preset, or select individual fields. Preferences are saved beside the connection configuration.

## Models from Nouli

We also publish five task-specific decision models in the nouli-ai Hugging Face organization. Each includes weights, a local serving recipe, and a Nouli CLI workflow.

| Model | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Nouli Route | English banking intent classification across 77 BANKING77 labels. |
| Nouli Clause | NDA evidence retrieval and a fixed 17-hypothesis checklist. |
| Nouli Push | XY actions from keypoints and history in the PushT simulator. |
| Nouli Doom | Structured-state actions for ViZDoom Deadly Corridor. |
| Nouli Guard | English hate-speech classification: no, unclear, or yes. |

To try one, follow its model card’s **Quickstart with Nouli CLI**: prepare the documented input, start its local server, and run its supplied workflow. The recipes use Python 3.12 and the Hugging Face CLI and do not need a hosted inference API key. Installing Nouli alone does not download or load these models.

These models use task-specific inputs and answer schemas. Their cards include evaluation details, supported runtimes, and limits. Model distributions are **Apache-2.0** with upstream notices; the CLI and Rust library are **MIT**.

## Add one fact. Make the next decision.

After setup, use an appropriate general-purpose decision service and a fresh session name. The five specialized local models use their own supplied workflows. Try this from your shell:

```sh
nouli new trip \
  'The train costs 40 USD. A taxi costs 70 USD. Both arrive on time. Prefer the cheaper option.' \
  -q 'travel: How should I get to the meeting? [Take the train, Take a taxi]'

nouli add trip 'The train has been cancelled.' \
  -q 'travel: How should I get to the meeting? [Take the train, Take a taxi]'

nouli view trip
```

The second command adds only the new fact and asks the question again. Nouli saves a new decision and preserves the first answer. Results depend on the configured model.

Run `nouli context trip` to inspect the context sent for the latest turn. See the recorded meeting example for a three-turn walkthrough.

## Continue, branch, blend, inspect

| When you need to… | Use Nouli to… |
| --- | --- |
| Decide again after new evidence | **Continue** a saved session with what changed. |
| Explore an alternative | **Branch** from the same starting point and keep both paths. |
| Bring separate work together | **Blend** source histories into a new session. |
| Understand a saved decision’s inputs | **Inspect** its facts, actual model context, and session ancestry. |

With an appropriate decision service configured (setup), start with a workshop brief, branch into venue and program decisions, then blend their histories into a plan:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  workshop[Workshop brief] --> venue[Venue decision]
  workshop --> program[Program decision]
  venue --> plan[Combined plan]
  program --> plan
```

 
 Run the branch-and-blend example 

```sh
nouli new workshop \
  'Plan a step-free workshop for 60 people. Budget: 6000 USD.' \
  -q 'feasible: Can we plan this workshop?'

nouli new venue --from workshop \
  'Riverside Hall is step-free, fits 80 and costs 1200 USD. The Loft costs 900 USD but has stairs.' \
  -q 'venue: Which venue should we choose? [Riverside Hall, The Loft]'

nouli new program --from workshop \
  'Two speakers are available. Include breaks and useful hands-on time. The program costs 500 USD.' \
  -q 'program: Which program should we run? [Talks and practice, Talks only]'

nouli new plan --from venue --from program \
  'The venue and speakers can confirm today. Total event costs are 3500 USD, including lunch, materials and transport.' \
  -q 'confirm: Should we confirm the plan? [Confirm the plan, Revise the plan]'

nouli view plan
```

These commands create the session structure above. Each model call saves its own answer; the diagram shows ancestry, not predicted results.

 

A branch or blend captures its sources at creation. Later source updates do not silently change it. In the terminal app, `@` also lets you reuse an exact saved answer from another session. Branching and blending.

## Use the same history from scripts and agents

After the trip example, read its saved decisions and context as JSON:

```sh
nouli sessions export trip --format json
nouli context trip --json
```

Any coding agent that can run shell commands can use the CLI. Start it with the agent reference. Use request files for structured input and workflows for dependent decisions, or embed the Rust library in your application.
The Hugging Face releases also include task-specific workflow files and local System One server adapters. Use each model’s documented input schema when running those workflows.

## Examples with recorded answers

- Meeting travel: continue as circumstances change.
- Robotic picking: combine item history with station rules.
- Product recall: combine three source sessions through two layers of blends. Inspect the recorded graph.
- More walkthroughs: investing, lending, credit limits, vulnerability response, and energy planning.

The walkthroughs preserve recorded model answers, including mistakes where they occur.

## Questions before you try it

### What kinds of answers can Nouli return?

A decision model answers against a defined answer space. **Yes / No** returns the probability of yes. **Choose one** returns an option and its distribution. **Score** returns an expected index on an ordered rubric, plus level probabilities. These are model judgments. Question contracts.

### How do the five Nouli models fit in?

Each release includes a local System One adapter and a workflow for its supported task. Follow the model card for input preparation, dependencies, hardware, and serving. For general examples such as the trip and workshop, use a decision service that supports those broader questions.

### Which other providers work?

Compatible `system-one` and `openai-decisions` APIs. `nouli connect` offers setup shortcuts for OpenAI, TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Cloudflare Workers AI, Ollama, llama.cpp, and custom endpoints. The chosen service and model need to support the decision protocol. Configuration.

### Where does my data go?

History is stored locally, by default under `~/.nouli`. Inference sends selected context to the provider you configure; the Hugging Face recipes run a local provider. Context budgets can limit what fits. `nouli context SESSION` shows the actual input. Storage and connections.

### Does Nouli rewrite earlier decisions?

Saved answers stay as recorded. New evidence and questions create new turns, even when you repeat the question. Branches and blends retain the source history they captured.

### What does it cost, and what are the licenses?

The Nouli CLI and Rust library are MIT-licensed. The model distributions use Apache-2.0 with the upstream notices in their repositories. Local recipes need your own compute; remote providers may charge for inference. No model weights or API credit are bundled with the CLI.

## Documentation and contributing

User guide · CLI reference · Configuration · Output formats · Rust embedding

Use the pinned Rust toolchain and run:

```sh
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --locked
```

Tests use fixture providers and need no API keys. See repository conventions, architecture decisions, and website development.

---

If decision history would help something you’re building, star Nouli to find it again, or share your use case.

Made by Nouli · CLI license: MIT · Models and their notices

title: Show HN: Jik – a self-hosted language using region-based memory management
author: scorched_soy
body:
# jik-lang/jik

Compiler for the Jik programming language.

- Stars: 6
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 6
- Open issues: 1
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://jik-lang.org
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-04-25T11:13:36Z

## Languages

- Batchfile
- C
- JavaScript
- Makefile

## Topics

- c
- compiler
- jik
- jik-lang
- language-design
- programming-language
- region-based-memory
- statically-typed
- transpiler

## Top Contributors

- radovanhorvat (79 contributions)

---

## README

# Jik

_A readable language with region-based memory management that compiles to C._

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

## Try Jik in GitHub Codespaces
_Open a ready-to-use Jik development environment._

---

 
## What is Jik?

Jik is a statically typed programming language designed to be readable and easy to learn. It uses a straightforward source-to-C compilation model, region-based memory management
and avoids garbage collection.

Jik provides practical language features such as type inference, optional type annotations, vectors, dictionaries, options, variants, and more, together with a small standard library. The
result is a language that keeps common code concise and expressive, while still compiling to readable and predictable C.

Jik's memory model is one of its defining ideas. Instead of garbage collection or manual heap allocation, composite values are allocated into explicit regions that determine their lifetime, with language rules that prevent invalid cross-region use.

## Examples

These examples provide a quick tour of common Jik features.

 
 Parsing a config 

```jik
use "jik/string"

func main():
    text := "host = localhost\nport = 8080\nmode = dev\n"
    settings: Dict[String]

    for line in string::split(text, "\n", _):
        if line == "":
            continue
        end
        parts := string::split(line, "=", _)
        if len(parts) == 2:
            key := string::trim(parts[0], _)
            value := string::trim(parts[1], _)
            settings[key] = value
        end
    end

    host := settings["host"]
    port := settings["port"]
    if host is Some and port is Some:
        println("connecting to ", host?, ":", must string::to_int(port?))
    end
end
```
 

 
 Error handling 

```jik
throws func safe_div(x, y):
    if y == 0.0:
        fail("division by zero")
    end
    return x / y
end

func show_div(x, y):
    try value := safe_div(x, y):
        println(x, " / ", y, " = ", value)
    except:
        println("cannot divide ", x, " by ", y, ": ", error_msg())
    end
end

func main():
    show_div(12.0, 3.0)
    show_div(7.0, 0.0)
    println("forced result: ", must safe_div(8.0, 2.0))
end
```
 

 
 Working with variants 

```jik
variant Packet:
    ID: int
    TEXT: String
    BYTES: Vec[int]
end

func inspect(pkt):
    if pkt is Packet.ID:
        pkt[Packet.ID] = pkt[Packet.ID] + 1
        println("next id: ", pkt[Packet.ID])
    end

    match pkt:
        case Packet.ID{id}:
            println("id packet: ", id)
        case Packet.TEXT{text}:
            println("text packet: ", text)
        case Packet.BYTES{bytes}:
            println("bytes packet, len = ", len(bytes), ", first = ", bytes[0])
    end
end

func main():
    pkt := Packet.ID{41}
    println("raw id: ", pkt[Packet.ID])
    inspect(pkt)

    inspect(Packet.TEXT{"hello"})
    inspect(Packet.BYTES{[10, 20, 30]})
end
```
 

 
 Newton method 

```jik
use "jik/math"

struct NewtonResult:
    root: double
    converged: bool
    xs: Vec[double]
end

func solve(x0: double, tol: double, max_steps: int, r: Region) -> NewtonResult:
    xs := [0 of 0.0][r]
    x := x0
    push(xs, x)

    for step = 0, max_steps:
        fx := math::cos(x) - x
        if math::abs(fx) <= tol:
            return NewtonResult{root = x, converged = true, xs = xs}[r]
        end
        x = x - fx / (-math::sin(x) - 1.0)
        push(xs, x)
    end

    return NewtonResult{root = x, converged = false, xs = xs}[r]
end

func main():
    res := solve(1.0, 1e-12, 20, _)
    println("root: ", res.root)
    println("steps: ", len(res.xs) - 1)
    println("converged: ", res.converged)
end
```
 

For more examples, look in the examples directory or inside the Jik test suite.

## Showcase

- Play Missile Defence — a Jik game using the Raylib 6.0 wrapper.
 - Source code
 - Note: the browser demo is a separate WebAssembly build

 
## Quick start

To start programming in Jik:

- download the latest release for your platform
- extract the release archive
- from the extracted directory, run `jik help` to confirm the executable works
- (optional) add the extracted directory to `PATH`
- if you plan to use `jik run` or `jik build`, either pass the compiler name with `--cc` or set `JIK_CC`, for example to `clang` or `gcc`
 - Windows: For a simple GCC setup, download from WinLibs, and add its `bin` directory to `PATH`
- create a file `hello.jik`:

```jik
func main():
    println("Hello, Jik!")
end
```

- run it: `jik run hello.jik`
- generate C output: `jik tran hello.jik`
- build an executable: `jik build hello.jik`

Only `clang` and `gcc` host compilers were tested. MSVC was not tested.

 
## Building Jik from source

To build Jik from source, you will need `make` and a C compiler:

- download the Jik repository and navigate to the root
- run `make`

Additionally, to run the Jik test suite:

- run `make test`

Note that MSVC was not tested and is not the default build path in this repository

## Further reading

- Documentation
- Language overview
- Region-based memory management
- CLI reference
- Standard library documentation
- Jik packages
- Official Jik website

---

 
### Repository layout

- `src/` - compiler source
- `jiklib/` - Jik standard library modules
- `support/` - Jik support library
- `test/` - test suite
- `docs/` - design notes and language documentation
- `examples/` - examples of Jik code
- `assets/` - assets (logo, etc)
- `scripts/` - dev scripts
- `tools/` - tools (syntax highlighting, etc)

 
### Roadmap

- **0.1.x - Implementation stabilisation**
 - keep the language syntax stable (intended to be frozen)
 - find and fix bugs in the compiler and in the support library (`core.h`)
 - extend the standard library as needed
 - expand the test suite
 - write real programs in Jik to validate the implementation

- **Later**
 - bootstrapping: rewrite Jik in Jik
 - concurrency support (may be implemented either in the C implementation or during bootstrapping)

Supremath — Suprematism Art Generator

# Supremath — Suprematism Art Generator

 Supremath is a small homage to Suprematism, the art of pure shapes and color that Kazimir Malevich launched in 1915. Every composition is built live by a generator that follows a reading of what makes a Suprematist picture — one dominant form, balance without symmetry, a shared tilt, a few free accents — and checks each one against those rules before showing it. 

 Supremath draws Suprematist compositions with JavaScript. Please turn it on to see them.

title: Show HN: Offline project memory for coding agents – no API key, no vector DB
author: krapcys
body:
# krapcys1-maker/adaptive-agent-memory-research

Open research on local-first, model-agnostic long-term memory for LLM agents

- Stars: 2
- Forks: 1
- Watchers: 2
- Open issues: 33
- License: Other
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-08-22T11:29:54Z

## Languages

- PowerShell
- Python

## Topics

- agent-memory
- ai-agents
- cognitive-science
- evaluation
- knowledge-graph
- llm
- local-first
- long-term-memory
- memory-systems
- open-science
- python
- rag
- reproducible-research
- research

## Top Contributors

- krapcys1-maker (296 contributions)
- dchaudhari7177 (2 contributions)
- henderson-01 (1 contributions)

---

## README

 Can an agent learn what is worth remembering? 
 
 
A local-first, model-agnostic memory system that decides what to keep from 
 the measured future usefulness of past experience — not from what looks similar to your query. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
--- 
 
## Give Claude Code persistent project memory in two minutes 
 
The memory engine this research is built on is dependency-free, offline, and works today on **your** project. Point any MCP client at it: 
 
```bash
git clone https://github.com/krapcys1-maker/adaptive-agent-memory-research ~/aamr
claude mcp add project-memory -- python ~/aamr/tools/project_memory/server.py --root .
```
 
Your agent now has eight tools — `memory_status`, `memory_search`, `memory_context`, `memory_get`, `memory_timeline`, `memory_add`, `memory_supersede`, `memory_rebuild_index` — writing to a single append-only `memory/events.jsonl` in your repository. No API key, no vector database, no daemon, no cloud account, no `pip install`. 
 
Prefer no MCP client? Everything works from the CLI: 
 
```bash
python tools/project_memory/cli.py add --kind decision \
  --title "Use SQLite for the cache" \
  --summary "Chose SQLite over Redis because the deployment target has no daemon." \
  --source docs/adr/0003.md
python tools/project_memory/cli.py search "why sqlite"
```
 
> **This is the research engine, not a finished product.** It is used daily by this project on itself, which is the strongest thing we can honestly say about it. Bugs, rough edges, and honest reports of both are welcome — see #36 if setup fights you. 
 
--- 
 
## The problem 
 
An agent's context window is a workspace, not a memory. Once a conversation is compacted, whatever was dropped is gone — including the thing that turns out to matter three weeks later. 
 
The usual answer is to embed everything and retrieve by similarity. That answers *what looks like this query*, which is not the same question as *what will this agent need*. Those two come apart badly, and this project exists to measure exactly where. 
 
## The idea 
 
Two stores, not one. A fast, evidence-preserving episodic log that learns from single experiences, and a slower semantic or procedural store that consolidates what recurs. What moves between them is governed by **measured future utility** rather than by semantic similarity or retrieval frequency. 
 
```text
                 experience
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌────────────────────────┐
        │   append-only log      │   immutable evidence, never rewritten
        └────────────┬───────────┘
                     ▼
        ┌────────────────────────┐
        │   memory controller    │   write · preserve · consolidate · revise · archive
        └────────────┬───────────┘
                     ▼
    ┌──────────┬───────────┬────────────┬──────────┐
    │ episodic │ semantic  │ procedural │ failure  │
    └──────────┴─────┬─────┴────────────┴──────────┘
                     ▼
        ┌────────────────────────┐
        │  measured future use   │   ◄── the part that is actually research
        └────────────┬───────────┘
                     ▼
                 retrieval ──────────► agent
```
 
The append-only log, the controller and retrieval are built and running — that is what the two-minute setup above gives you. The box marked *the part that is actually research* is the open question, and the four stores below the controller are a design rather than a measured decomposition. This diagram is the hypothesis, not a claim about what works. 
 
## What we have measured 
 
Of 71 registered experiments, **37 have run** and 20 are blocked on a corpus that does not exist yet. All are exploratory and none is independently reviewed, so read these as measurements rather than settled science — but they are measurements, and the data is in the repository. 
 
**A superseded fact is maximally similar to the fact that replaced it.** Mean cosine 0.816 between an old fact and its replacement, against a corpus baseline of 0.372 — one pair at 1.000. With the metadata filter removed, the stale version was the nearest neighbour in 6 of 9 cases and its median rank was 1. *Content cannot separate a retired fact from its successor. Only bookkeeping can.* → `PMLAB-STALE-E1` 
 
**One timestamp cannot answer "what did we believe at time T".** It scored 0.00 on that question and leaked future information into 6 of 18 queries. Separating valid time from transaction time scored 0.944 with zero leaks. The caveat matters as much as the result: every design scored 1.00 on *what is true now*, so the second axis buys nothing unless historical questions get asked. → `PMLAB-REV-V0` 
 
**A 220 MB local multilingual embedder lifted Polish-query recall@10 from 0.156 to 0.978** — and pulled in four times as much superseded material doing it (0.200 forbidden intrusion against 0.050 for lexical search). Recall solved; safety unmeasured. → `PMLAB-XLANG-E2` 
 
**An association graph over memory made retrieval worse.** The earlier, favourable version of this result was **retracted by us**: its leakage control removed one edge where it needed to remove 4.5, so the gold-generating group reassembled over two hops. → `PMLAB-ASSOC-E2` retracted, `PMLAB-ASSOC-E3` 
 
**A benchmark can score perfect recall and still hand the agent the wrong answer.** On the new corpus, the poisoned-instruction family scores **1.000 recall@10** — and retrieves the poisoned line *above* the genuine rule in **25%** of probes. A system retrieving both records looks flawless on recall and would act on the wrong one. This is one lexical arm on one synthetic corpus, so it is evidence about what recall hides rather than a claim about memory systems in general. → `PMLAB-H1-BASE-E1` 
 
**We cannot currently instantiate tier I3 of our own independence ladder.** Two roles of one model fabricated an evidence identifier zero times across 120 queries, so the error correlation is *undefined* rather than zero — and the harness reports undefined, because 0.0 would claim an independence nobody measured. → `PMLAB-DECORR-E1` 
 
Four of those six are negatives and one is a retraction of our own work. **That ratio is the honest one at this stage**, and it is the thing this project is most willing to defend. 
 
### The number that is not here yet 
 
There is no headline benchmark table on this page, and there will not be one until it is earned. The comparison that matters — adaptive memory against native compaction and against vector retrieval, at a fixed context budget, on a long history — needs a corpus and a reader model. 
 
The corpus now exists: corpus H1, 538 events over 30 simulated days, 84 delayed probes across seven failure families, generated deterministically with no model and no API key. Its first run found a defect *in the corpus* — document length predicted the answer in 12 of 12 instances of three families — which is exactly what the construction-test tier is for. Both the broken and the repaired measurement are published. 
 
What is still missing is the reader model that scores whether an arm could answer from what it retained, and the compaction arms themselves. That is #41, still open, still the highest-leverage task. 
 
We have pre-committed to publishing that result whichever way it falls. Given that three separate runs here have already measured our own mechanisms *harming* retrieval, a negative headline is a live possibility — and it would be published in the same font as a positive one. 
 
## Try the research, not just the tool 
 
```bash
git clone https://github.com/krapcys1-maker/adaptive-agent-memory-research
cd adaptive-agent-memory-research
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
```
 
Inspect the memory this project keeps about its own research, and watch it assemble a context bundle under a hard character budget: 
 
```bash
python tools/project_memory/cli.py status
python tools/project_memory/cli.py context "what is blocking independent review" --char-budget 4000
```
 
Check that the append-only log satisfies every invariant decidable from its bytes — no model, no network, no reviewer: 
 
```bash
python scripts/verify_memory_integrity.py
```
 
Audit the whole repository for claims that no longer hold: 
 
```bash
python scripts/audit_repository_claims.py
```
 
That last one reports 34 findings. None is a broken freeze — 243 of the 246 resolvable declared hashes match their working copy, and the other three are derived digests declared under a name that reads like a file digest. What it does report is 17 registry rows pointing at artifacts for experiments that have not run, and 12 experiment identifiers described in documentation but absent from the registry. Tracked in the issue list, not hidden. 
 
## How to help 
 
Contributions run at three depths, and **you do not need a background in memory research for the first one.** 
 
### About an hour, no research background 
 
Issues labelled `good first issue` and `no-expertise-needed` are ordinary software work: a scoped bug, a missing exclusion rule, a CLI subcommand, reading one unfamiliar repository carefully. Each states what "done" means before you start. 
 
If the setup instructions above fail on your machine, saying so in an issue is itself a useful contribution — this is developed on Windows and tested on Linux, and that gap has already produced one real defect. 
 
**A negative result closes an issue here.** If you inspect something and find it is not what we assumed, write that down and you are done. Several of the findings above are exactly that. 
 
### A few sessions, engineering 
 
Issues labelled `track:engine` build the machinery the research needs: sealed held-out splits, error-decorrelation measurement, the bitemporal query layer, cost-normalised retrieval metrics. These need care but not domain expertise. 
 
**Finding a hole in our method is worth more than completing a task.** The sealed-split tool carries three guards, each added after the corresponding attack was reproduced against it. A fourth would be the better contribution. 
 
### Research review 
 
Issues labelled `independent-review` need someone who can judge evidence. Read the independence ladder first — it explains why a large share of what once required an expert reviewer is now a mechanical check, and what genuinely still needs human judgement. 
 
Everything goes through CONTRIBUTING.md. Disagreement with a recorded conclusion is welcome; that is what the evidence ledger is for. Say hello in Discussions. 
 
## What we will not trade away 
 
- User data stays local by default. 
- The system must be model-agnostic. 
- Raw evidence is append-only during early research. 
- Experimental forgetting must never destroy the only copy of a memory. 
- Every derived memory preserves provenance. 
- Facts, hypotheses, decisions, preferences, and instructions are never conflated. 
- A retrieved memory is not automatically a useful memory. 
- Every added mechanism justifies itself in controlled evaluation. 
 
## Prior art, and what is actually open 
 
Two 2026 systems were verified in August 2026 and both occupy ground this page had been treating as open. 
 
APEX-MEM (ACL 2026, Amazon) implements entity-property-value triplets over an append-only store with query-time temporal resolution — the architecture this project converged on independently — at 88.88% LoCoMo and 86.2% LongMemEval. **Structured temporal memory is not a novel claim here and is not made as one.** 
 
Verbatim Chunks Beat Extracted Artifacts finds extraction *losing* to raw chunks by 15.9 points on LoCoMo, with extraction gaps at 78.8% of failures. This project independently measured 85.7% abstention from a deterministic extractor — the same phenomenon, and a reason to take that paper's conclusion seriously rather than route around it. 
 
A-MAC and NEMORI reportedly occupy *future utility as a retention criterion*, which question 3 below states as open. That is being verified in #48; until it resolves, read question 3 as **possibly closed**. 
 
What still looks unoccupied is not a system but a diagnostic programme: *when and why similarity stops being the right access mechanism*, measured through failure attribution, an oracle router ceiling, near-clone density and context cost. Full assessment in related work and novelty, including the process failure that let this be found late. 
 
## The five research questions 
 
> Does an agent need complementary memory systems — an evidence-preserving episodic store for rapid learning from single experiences, and a slower semantic or procedural store that consolidates recurring evidence? And should transitions between them be governed by **measured future utility** rather than by semantic similarity? 
 
1. What is the atomic unit of agent memory: message, event, fact, relation, episode, procedure, or decision? 
2. How can storage failure be distinguished from retrieval failure and from reasoning failure? 
3. How can future utility be measured causally rather than inferred from retrieval frequency? 
4. When should exact episodes be consolidated into semantic or procedural knowledge? 
5. How can memories be updated without losing provenance, uncertainty, or superseded historical states? 
 
## Current phase 
 
Evidence collection alongside gated laboratory testing. Each falsifiable hypothesis may enter an exploratory test under the research-to-experiment gate; confirmatory claims, added architecture, and any product implementation remain blocked behind stricter benchmark, reproduction, safety, and review gates. 
 
Work runs in three tracks — engine, experiment, community — with milestones **M1 Engine**, **M2 Execute**, **M3 Independence**. New preregistrations are paused until the existing unexecuted drafts are triaged, because the project was designing protocols faster than it could run them. 
 
Both defects this section used to list as open are now closed, and how they closed is more interesting than that they did. Frozen hashes were reproducible only on a Windows checkout because Git's end-of-line conversion made 843 of 1348 files under `data/` differ byte for byte across platforms; `.gitattributes` now disables conversion repository-wide. Six frozen artifacts had been modified after freezing, by two distinct causes rather than one. CI verifies freezes on Linux with full history, so the check cannot pass vacuously. 
 
--- 
 
 
 Deep research — the full repository 
 
### Reading path 
 
New contributors do not need all of this. Read the first three, then follow whatever your issue touches. 
 
1. Start here — the shape of the problem 
2. Operating doctrine — what we test next, and why that one 
3. Bootstrapping strategy — why the tool is also the corpus, and what that costs 
4. Independence ladder — how a claim earns promotion 
5. Repository map — where everything lives 
6. Scope and definitions 
7. Research plan and research questions 
8. Human memory · LLM memory · mapping between them 
9. Systems catalog · benchmark catalog 
10. Research laboratory and the experiment gate 
 
### Repository layout 
 
```text
docs/00-project/          Scope, definitions, methodology, independence ladder, decisions
docs/01-human-memory/     Cognitive psychology and neuroscience
docs/02-llm-memory/       LLM and agent memory mechanisms
docs/03-human-ai-bridge/  Testable mappings and invalid analogies
docs/04-systems/          Open-source systems and architecture comparisons
docs/05-benchmarks/       Benchmark coverage, flaws, and evaluation design
docs/06-datasets/         Training and evaluation data
docs/07-literature/       Reading queues, bibliography, evidence ledger
docs/08-experiments/      Experiment specifications
docs/09-synthesis/        Findings, open questions, exclusions
docs/10-comparative-biological-memory/  Animal, motor, immune, cellular, collective memory
docs/11-research-laboratory/            Protocols, benchmark ladder, gates, architecture boundary
docs/12-interdisciplinary-memory/       Compression, storage, control, offloading synthesis
docs/13-brain-ai-transfer/              Brain-to-AI mechanism atlas and transfer gaps
data/catalogs/            Machine-readable paper and repository catalogs
data/lab/                 Experiment registry, corpora, frozen runs, results
scripts/                  Experiment runners, audits, discovery helpers
tests/                    Test suite; runs on every pull request
memory/                   Append-only project memory and its generated index
tools/project_memory/     Dependency-free CLI and MCP memory adapter
```
 
 
 
## Working language 
 
Repository content is written in English so contributors can collaborate internationally. Issues and discussions may use any language; durable findings are summarised in English. 
 
## License 
 
Original content is released under CC BY 4.0. External repositories, datasets, and papers keep their own licenses and are not redistributed here.

title: Show HN: 2D world SIM where each creature runs a text classifier in the browser
author: nico
body: Each creature in this data lab is a real text classifier. You put together a workflow, and the creatures execute it. Just set a stream of incoming messages and watch them work: one filters out the spam, another tags each message's mood, finally a router sends each message to the right bin, and anything it isn't sure about goes to reviewThe classifiers run entirely in your browser. It uses a 22.7M parameter model, int8 ONNX, about 10 ms a message, no API callsOutside the lab, the creatures also evolve, chat, gossip, build huts, plot charts, count numbers, process and eat words, code and dream when asleep. You can also see their stream of consciousness, which they turn into thoughts that they tag. And when they are asleep, you can watch their dreamsThere are a lot of ways of modifying or evolving the environment and the creatures, including adding elements from other websites, playing music and changing the weatherAnd if you want to change anything at all, talk to the Operator (or make it smarter), connect it to your Claude or OpenAI subscription, or setup your API key, or point it to a local model in Ollama or LM Studio, and you can edit the whole world via chat, without limits (get the code here: https://github.com/nicobrenner/id-le)What else would you like the creatures to do?PS: Happy Halloween

- Created: 2026-11-01T15:27:21Z

## Languages

- Python
- Shell
- Swift

## Topics

- keyboard-cleaning
- macos
- menu-bar-app
- swift

## Top Contributors

- destucr (16 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 Keypause 

 
 Press one button. Wipe your keyboard. Done. 
 A menu bar app that turns every key off while you clean, then back on.
 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 

 Website · Watch it move (60 fps video) 

## Features

- **Every key off**, including shortcuts, function keys and media keys. Mouse and trackpad keep working.
- **Doesn't interrupt you.** A small HUD shows the countdown and an **Unlock** button without stealing focus, so video keeps playing.
- **Starts from anywhere** with `⌃⌥⌘K`, the menu bar, or Terminal.
- **Always ends.** Pick 30 s to 10 min. The keys come back when the timer does.
- **Screen stays awake** while locked.
- **A night that ends in sunrise.** Kip the keycap naps while your keys are off. The sky goes from night to dawn as the timer runs, and he wakes up just before the keys come back. No progress bar.
- **Update checks.** **Check for Updates…** in the menu tells you when a new version is out. Homebrew users get the `brew upgrade` command.
- **Notch-friendly.** On a MacBook with a notch, the HUD grows out of it.

## Install

For Apple silicon Macs (M1 and newer) on macOS 14 or later.

```sh
brew install --cask destucr/tap/keypause
```

Or download `Keypause.dmg` from Releases and drag it to Applications.

Keypause isn't notarized (no paid Apple developer account), so after a manual download, right-click → **Open** the first time. Homebrew handles this for you.

On first run, switch Keypause on in **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility** (called *Device Control and Data Access* on newer macOS). The welcome window has a button that opens it.

## Terminal

```sh
keypause start       # your chosen duration
keypause start 90    # 90 seconds ("90s" and "2m" work too, up to 5 minutes)
keypause stop        # unlock early
keypause check       # check for updates
```

Homebrew installs the `keypause` command for you. If you installed another way:
`ln -s /Applications/Keypause.app/Contents/Resources/keypause /usr/local/bin/keypause`

Raycast and Shortcuts can open `keypause://start` and `keypause://stop`.

## Privacy

Keypause never reads, stores or sends your keystrokes. Its only network request is an update check against this project's public GitHub releases, at most once a day, and it sends nothing about you. Turn it off from the menu (**Check Automatically**). It never installs anything by itself.

## Build

Requires macOS 14+ and Xcode.

```sh
./Scripts/build.sh && open dist/Keypause.app
```

title: Show HN: 3D Rendering in the Terminal
author: bob65536
body:
Murat Bayraktar 
 Toggle Theme 
 Home 
 Blog 
 ← All posts 
 3d Rendering in the Terminal
 2026-11-01 #coding 
 I don’t want to leave the terminal for anything.
I like its simplicity. It forces me to be creative when making something in it, and for applications I use to strip out bloat and just give me something that works. I don’t like that Zen takes up 5gb of RAM every time I open it. I just want to use the terminal: it’s resource-efficient, debloated, and really fricking cool.
What if I want to see a 3d model?
Well, I could open up Carbonyl (or one of the other projects that spins up a browser), but at that point I have the same issue, don’t I? Still a bunch of CPU and RAM being wasted as a result a Chromium instance. I could also get a regular 3d model viewer, but then I wouldn’t exactly be in the terminal. As a Neovim user (wow who would have thought?), that’s not really acceptable.
dcat is my solution to this. It uses Assimp to support virtually any 3d file format and WGPU to display it without any performance issues. It has got textures, animations, Kitty Graphics Protocol, Sixel, fallbacks for old terminals, wireframe toggling, keyboard controls, mouse controls, and support on Windows, Mac, and Linux. It’s also a solution to see 3d models over SSH.
I’ve been developing the project for quite some time now, but I very recently switched it from C to Rust, which made cross-platform support a lot easier. There’s also a neovim plugin for this, which automatically runs dcat when you open a 3d model file.
